At the end of the tram line, where the city gave up pretending to be a city and became a field with opinions, there was a shop that repaired things no one else would touch.

Not watches or shoes. There were perfectly good shops for those.

The sign in the window read:

**APOLOGIES RESTORED**  
**BAD ENDINGS ALTERED**  
**SMALL MISUNDERSTANDINGS WHILE YOU WAIT**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**No miracles. Please stop asking.**

The proprietor was a woman named Ada, who wore a carpenter’s apron and kept her pencils in a chipped vase. Most mornings she worked on minor repairs: a joke that had landed cruelly, a goodbye spoken while looking at a phone, a birthday forgotten for reasons that were understandable but not good enough.

People brought these things in paper bags.

They often said, “It’s probably nothing.”

Ada would open the bag.

“Well,” she would say, “let’s have a look.”

One wet Thursday, a man arrived carrying nothing at all.

“I think I’ve wasted my life,” he said.

Ada glanced at the clock. It was twenty minutes until closing.

“That’s a large item.”

“I know.”

“Have you brought the whole thing?”

He looked down at his empty hands.

“I wouldn’t know how.”

She pulled out a chair.

“Start with yesterday.”

Yesterday, he told her, he had done laundry. He had answered six emails and avoided a seventh. He had eaten lunch standing up. On the way home, he had stopped to watch two men trying to get a sofa through a narrow doorway.

“Did they manage it?” Ada asked.

“I don’t know. I went home.”

“What was in the seventh email?”

“An invitation. My brother wants me to visit.”

“And do you want to?”

“Yes. But we haven’t spoken properly in years. I keep trying to write something that explains.”

Ada took a small envelope from beneath the counter and slid it across to him.

He opened it. Inside was a tram ticket.

“What does this repair?”

“Nothing yet. Your brother lives three stops from here, doesn’t he?”

“Four.”

“You’ll have to pay the difference.”

He remained in the chair for a while, turning the ticket over. Then he asked if he could borrow a pencil.

Ada gave him one from the vase. On the back of an old receipt, he wrote several sentences, crossed them out, and finally took out his phone.

“Can I come on Saturday?” he read aloud.

Ada was putting away her tools.

“You’d have to ask him.”

After he left, she found the pencil tucked behind her ear. Outside, the last of the rain dripped from the awning, and a tram waited at the edge of the field with its doors open.
